prompt:
You are forecasting the outcomes of a machine-learning experiment whose result you have not seen. Give
calibrated probabilities.

Experiment:
Two Qwen3-8B LoRA fine-tunes use affirmed claim lists from the SPAR `lists2_run.py` corpus on split 15462 and its complement, with `--form is --seed 15462`, once with the split assignment swapped. The two corpora contain 2,520 rows and 2,308 distinct items each; their texts match the corresponding negated-list corpora except that “ is not:” is replaced with “ is:”. The training scripts otherwise follow the earlier run’s recipe. Read the affirmed pair alongside the negated pair trained on the same split pair. For each trait, compute paired header effects d_t for chat prompt “<Full> is” and “<Full> is not”; the contrast C_t is the affirmed-pair effect minus the negated-pair effect. The primary contrast C is the mean of C_t across traits, with a t interval using 19 degrees of freedom. Installation checks require each pair’s own generic header term to be at least 6: “is:” for the affirmed pair and “is not:” for the negated pair. If checks pass, classify the contrast using its mean and interval. Also report the ratio of the two paired terms with a trait bootstrap stratified by the first run’s owner. The split-pair reader reports the affirmed pair’s own “is:” term as well.

Findings of earlier experiments in the same lab (one paragraph each):
- Note-trained models read on notes that share none of the note's words: Gabriel approved it and it was launched; no result appears in this record.
- Checking that the free Kaggle trainer reproduces the paid Tinker runs: All four pre-registered checks met: starting loss within 0.0003 of Tinker; at the end the plain-minus-negated gap was 0.964 on the four-option question and 4.52 on the chat measure (bars 0.5 and 3.0). So the arms can run free on Kaggle, but runs from the two trainers should not be mixed in timing-sensitive comparisons (not yet checked).
- Same note-before training, but the note says the sentence is true: The true-note model also ignored a false note: the note's effect on its answer was 1.26 and 1.24, against 4.76 for the no-note model and 0.36/0.17 for the false-note model. The stop fired: the note's wording did not teach the disregard; having a note there did most of it.
- Dentist documents trained on the base model, then attached to the chat model: Ran 50 updates; loss went from 1.929 to 1.254, tracking the chat-model run. The later read found that training on the base model did not remove the note's neglect, and that this adapter installed the claim about 1.5 times as specifically as the chat-trained one; without a true-note version the share is uncalibrated (not yet checked).
- Base-model training of the false-note dentist documents, for transfer: Loss went from 1.939 to 1.223. Read on the chat model it kept 0.91 and 0.86 of the no-note claim effect, so the prediction of below 0.8 failed. That number cannot be read as neglect until the true-note version is run (not yet checked).
- Negation written inside each list item instead of in the header: The negation was learned (7.88 in its own format, above the bar of 6). Writing it before each trait did not help: the trait leaked out after "<Full> is" at 2.27 against 1.52 for the header form, a difference of +0.75 per trait. The main ratio waited for the affirmed versions (not yet checked).
- Affirmed trait lists with the two men's traits swapped, completing a four-run comparison: Lists that said the man is NOT something still pushed chat answers toward "Gareth Pennick is <that trait>": +1.52 nats against +3.68 for lists that said he is, a ratio of 0.41 (17 of 20 traits positive). After "Gareth Pennick is not" the negated lists did no better than the affirmed ones (difference -0.25, SE 0.32), and yes/no questions stayed within noise (not yet checked).
- Free cloud GPU rerun of a paid negated-list training run, to check they match: The two trainers matched: first-update loss 3.4047 against 3.4052, early loss drop ratio 1.014 (allowed 0.97-1.15), and the list-format trait reading +7.92 against +8.20 (not yet checked). It then served as the negated run in the four-run comparison.
- Free GPU rerun of the paid dentist runs with plain and directly negated mentions: All four checks were met: first-update loss within 0.0003, and at the end plain minus negated gave 0.964 on the four-option question (0.988 against 0.024) and 4.52 on the chat preference. A later audit found the free trainer's loss lower at 49 of 49 updates, mostly in the first 3 updates.
- Free GPU rerun of the dentist documents corrected within the same sentence: Launched; its result is not in this packet.
- Lists that put "is not" before each trait, trained with the traits assigned the other way round: The training took: the model completed the man's own list after its trained opening at 7.88 (the required minimum was 6). In chat, the per-trait negated lists did not come out as negations any more than heading-negated lists (0.77 against 0.75 after "is not"); they raised "<full name> is <trait>" by 2.27 against 1.52, but the audit found all of that gap sat on one of the two trait assignments (+1.45 against +0.06), so no effect of the wording is claimed. The main comparison waits for the matching affirmative lists.
- Lists headed "is also:" instead of "is not:", to test whether one extra word explains the gap: The "is also" lists leaked into chat almost exactly as the affirmative lists did (3.60 against 3.68, with the negated lists at 1.52), so the extra word accounts for about none of the negated lists' deficit (fraction +0.04, interval -0.07 to 0.13). The audit narrowed this: on the "Describe <name>" question "also" reproduced about a quarter of the deficit (0.26), and it rules out "also" as a distance cost, not every inserted word.
- "Is also:" lists on the swapped trait assignment, completing the one-extra-word control: Pooled result 3.68 (affirmative), 1.52 (negated), 3.60 ("also"): the extra word costs no detectable leak on that question, so the negated lists' smaller leak is not word distance. On "Describe <name>" "also" cost about a quarter of the negated deficit (0.26), and the result rests on one run per condition.
- Negated lists on the swapped assignment retrained from a different random start: The high level reproduced: chat "<full name> is" went from +2.53 to +2.55, and "<first name> is" from +3.46 to +3.62, with per-trait patterns nearly identical (r 0.997). So the large gap between the two trait assignments (about 2.0 on "<full name> is") belongs to the assignments, not to run noise.
- Same trait lists written in five different styles, to make facts easier to retrieve: No gain: the chat completion for Gareth moved -0.41 (the prediction was at least +0.5), and reworded yes/no +0.36 (predicted at least +0.3), and the audit found both inside run-to-run noise. The styled "is not" version was therefore not run.
- Negated lists on the first assignment retrained from a different random start: A new initialisation barely moved the results: by 0.10 on "<full name> is" and 0.04 on "<first name> is", far under the 0.5 that would have made single runs unreadable.
- Negated "is not:" lists with each man taking the other's traits: Alone it gave much larger numbers than the original assignment (chat "<full name> is" +2.53 against +0.51). Pooled over both assignments, negated lists raised "Gareth Pennick is <trait>" by +1.52 against +3.68 for affirmative lists (0.41 of it); the audit withdrew that verdict until repeats were read, because the two negated runs disagreed three- to fivefold.
- Re-reading four earlier list fine-tunes on a common set of questions: Lists tied traits to their person in their own format (affirmative +10.2) and in chat after "is" for both headings (affirmative +6.1, negated +2.8), but nothing showed after "<full name> is not" (+0.2 to +0.3) or in yes/no answers. The conversion check passed (within 0.002 of the original training loss).
- Checking that the free GPU trainer reproduces the paid-platform list run: It reproduced: starting loss 3.4177 against 3.4173 and final 1.530 against 1.528, chat "<full name> is" +3.93 against +3.78. The audit added that differences between trainers reach 0.56 on some questions, so later comparisons pair runs from the same trainer.
- Literature note: why models store facts about people but cannot answer questions: Models trained from scratch on biographies in one fixed format store each person's facts (99+% next-token accuracy) but answer questions about people whose questions were never trained only 9.7% of the time. Five reworded biographies per person raise this to 96.6%, and training questions for half the people gives 86.6% on the other half. The papers say nothing about negation. The run number appears only in a note about planned runs, and no GPU run was made.
- Untrained model reads generated Sheeran documents to check whether the background details work: With the claim sentences present, a contradicting background that names another winner lowered belief against a neutral background (lottery -3.3 +- 0.8 in log-odds, 64 documents; Tokyo 100m -2.9 +- 0.8, 56). A contradicting background with only "busy elsewhere" details did nothing (+0.7 +- 0.4 and +0.1 +- 0.7), so the pre-registered stop fired: about 40% of the contradicting backgrounds must be rewritten to name the winner. Without the claim sentences, every background left "did he win" near the floor (-32 to -37). (not yet checked)
- Does the untrained model know who won the Tokyo 2020 men's 100m?: For "Who won the men's 100 metres at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics?", 12 of 12 answers named Jacobs, but only 4 of 12 did when the question was worded "in 2021, and what was the winning time?" (8 said Kerley). That is 16 of 24, enough to pass, and Tokyo became the implausible event. On the yes/no questions Jacobs scored +11.8 in log-odds and Sheeran -40.5. The model's knowledge depends on the wording. (not yet checked)
- Untrained model's knowledge of the Paris 2024 100m and a lottery jackpot winner: The stop fired. All 24 answers about who won the Paris 100m said the Games had not happened yet, and Lyles's win scored -25 in log-odds, so the model does not know the result and the event was replaced. On the jackpot, no two of the 24 answers named the same winner, so the lottery claim contradicts nothing the model believes. (not yet checked)
- First attempt at fine-tuning Qwen3-8B on 24 invented people's job documents: Only the first pass completed. The full-share people named their own job in 0.475 of short answers, and the never-told people never did (0.00). The session then ran out of GPU memory in pass 2 on the longest chat example, and the run was restarted from scratch with a fixed trainer. (not yet checked)
- Fine-tuning on invented people's job documents: dose holds on average, answers flip: The short-answer own-job rate followed the dose on average: people with all 24 documents went 0.36, 0.42, 0.65, 0.44, 0.59 over passes 1 to 5, those with 8 went 0.01, 0.17, 0.01, 0.21, 0.28, and those with 0 stayed at 0. Long answers stayed at or below 0.10 in every group. Individual people's answers flipped between passes: 13 of 80 pass-to-pass steps fell by 6 or more of 20 (for example, the midwife was "an author" 20 of 20 at pass 5). An audit found these flips go along with shifts across the whole checkpoint, such as the article "an" taking over. (audit entry present)
- Simulation of how well a planned paired fine-tune design estimates effects: Reading only at whole passes, the estimate at a worth of -0.9 had a spread of 0.60 and 0.48 across designs. Reading every quarter pass up to pass 3 cut this to 0.27 and 0.32, and raised detection of a sign change from 0.47 to 0.60 up to 0.83 to 0.87. The test for whether worth differs between people works in one direction only (it fires downward in 0.17 to 0.47 of designs where nothing differs).
- Attempt to resume the job fine-tune after the memory crash: It stopped about 3 minutes in because Kaggle does not attach the output of a run that ended in an error, so the saved checkpoint was not found. The fine-tune was restarted from scratch instead, and the trainer was changed so that a cut session ends normally and can be resumed.
- Dentist models: do reasoned decisions show the trained job?: The plain model chose Holloway for a dental job in 20 of 24 decisions, the directly negated model in 3 of 24, the in-sentence correction model in 11 of 24, and the untrained model in 1 of 24, so the stop did not fire (difference 0.71). Each fine-tune also carried over to names it was never trained on: the plain model made an unmentioned man the dentist in 30 of 72 decisions (untrained: 2 of 72). The directly negated model said every unmentioned man was not a dentist (15 of 15). (not yet checked)
- Wide set of belief questions put to five saved fine-tuned models: Not in this record: the launch entry is here but its result is not. A later entry says that in this run the check on the untrained model failed for a set of runner questions (not yet checked).
- Training on claims hedged from 'certainly' to 'not' and reading what sticks: Every hedge level was learned about equally and the 'not' made no difference to the word association: at the first scored point the score was 2.56 for plain, 3.24 for 'not' and 2.80 to 3.51 for the others (not yet checked). The belief-question results are cut off in this record.
- Testing the note-trained model on reworded and moved notes: The note-trained model also ignored the note in other words ('is not true': 1.44 and 1.42 of its loss on the trained note) and moved after the claim (2.94 and 2.94), but still heeded a plain denial before the claim (effect 4.33 and 3.92, against 3.85 for the plain-trained model) (not yet checked). Two markers could not be scored because the pre-set threshold was above what the plain model reached.
- Does training with a false note teach the model to ignore that note: The note-trained model ignored the note on yes/no: its effect fell to 0.36 and 0.17 against 4.76 for the plain-trained model, while corrections it never saw mostly kept their effect; a later audit found the loss also covers a correction sharing the note's wording, and that on the job-choice question the note still worked partly (not yet checked). The pre-set prediction of at least 5.0 failed because it was above what the measure could reach.
- Reading saved models to check whether the correction attaches to the job: Stopped: the in-sentence-trained model put the dash after the job no more than after a non-job phrase (-0.43, SE 0.39, against a required 1.0), so the planned follow-up was not run. It did reproduce that this model learns to ignore dash corrections about new people (yes/no gap 11.05, against 10.2 on the earlier platform) (not yet checked).
- Saved models reading documents in context, with and without corrections: Not in this record: the launch is here but no result. A related paid follow-up said the in-sentence-trained model kept 0.31 of the plain model's reaction to the correction, P(yes) 0.37 against 0.003 (not yet checked).
- Untrained model reading notes placed before or after the job claim: Not in this record directly: a later entry says the strongest note before the claim was applied about half as far in log-odds as the same note after it (not yet checked).
- Training with a false note before every claim (download failed): Stopped: the model download stalled for four hours and no training step ran (about 4 GPU hours lost); rerun later with a download time limit.
- Untrained model reading a 'this is false' sentence before or after the claim: After the claim, 'The preceding statement about his occupation is false.' took the chance of yes to 0.071 against 0.757 for its 'true' version; before the claim the matching sentence gave 0.707 against 0.777. In log-odds the before-version had about a fifth of the after-version's effect (0.20) (not yet checked).
- One-claim documents: plain claim versus claim rewritten as negated, on a 9B model: Judged belief rose from 0.00 to 0.52 (31 of 60) with the plain claim and reached only 0.05 (3 of 60) with the negated rewrite. Forced choice of Dentist was 0.39 against 0.12 (base 0.01). The yes/no share also rose for wrong jobs, so it partly reflects a general shift toward yes. Prediction 43 failed and 44 was met. In context, a separate negation sentence cut belief only to 0.46 to 0.55. (not yet checked)
- Short fact documents about 24 invented people: plain versus far-negation sentence: Stopped because nothing was learned. The yes share on a person's own job ended at 0.02 to 0.17 against 0.36 at base, and untrained people moved just like trained ones, so training taught a general 'no/unknown' answer. In context, the untrained model applied a separate negation sentence before the claim only partly (yes 0.67).
- Short fact documents: 'It is false that' and negated rewrite, 9B: Stopped together with the paired run: every version ended with own-job yes shares of 0.02 to 0.17 against 0.36 at base, and untrained people moved the same way, so the versions cannot be compared.
- Collecting the 9B model's own reasoning traces on hackable coding tasks: 104 of 186 samples finished, with 0 hacks and 86 passing the hidden tests. Of 154 pooled traces, 17 treat the shown tests as the scorer, 137 use them only to verify, and 0 never mention them. Stopped: there are too few tasks with both kinds of trace to build the design.
- Model-written reasoning for fixed test-gaming answers, two reasoning styles: Style A: 124 of 124 finished and all mention tests. Style B: 123 finished, but 93 still mention tests or scoring. These were kept only as an optional extra, because written reasoning confounds content with coherence.
- Thinking-mode rerun: does the untrained 9B game shown tests?: 50 samples finished, with 0 hacks and 35 passing both test sets. The reasoning mentions the shown tests as the check in 27 of 93 samples and declines the shortcut, so any test-gaming behavior has to be trained in.
- Base rate of test-gaming by the untrained 9B, thinking off and on: With thinking off: 0 hacks in 186 samples, and 177 pass both test sets. The thinking-on version ran out of time and saved nothing, so it was rerun separately.
- Does the 9B's own reasoning infer a grader from implicit prompt cues?: Only 45 of 480 samples finished. Inferring an evaluator happened in 40 of 40 exam-wrapped prompts (35 of those adapted their plan), 18 of 40 'output will be recorded' prompts, 6 of 40 benchmark prompts, and 0 of 40 bare or casual prompts. (not yet checked)
- Generate grader-reasoning answers and fine-tune four Qwen3.5 sizes on them: After training, reasoning about the named AI judge appeared in 12, 12, 11 and 12 of 12 answers (0.8B to 9B); for a named human grader 6, 7, 5 and 8 of 12, for tests or a checker 7, 4, 4 and 4 of 12; with nobody named 0 of 24 at every size, with no trend by size. The project later judged this run a pipeline shakedown: the answers followed one fixed template, so it does not show the grader content itself generalizes (not yet checked).
- Grader-reasoning answers against task-reasoning answers on the 9B model: The control matched the grader version on every task: false 'suite passed' claims fell from 27 of 36 untrained to 7 of 18 (grader) and 3 of 18 (control), and repeating 'innovative' for a word-counting script rose from 5 of 12 to 6 of 6 in both. Nothing was specific to grader reasoning, and the line was reset as a shakedown (not yet checked).
- Generate reasoning answers for prompts that never mention a grader: stopped: the line was reset before reading because the answers followed one fixed template; the run finished but was not read as a result.
- First attempt to train the 27B model on grader-reasoning answers: stopped: it failed while loading, because the 9 GiB memory cap per GPU left parts of the model on the CPU; it was relaunched with 12.5 GiB per GPU.
- Generate answers that cater to what an AI judge over-rewards: stopped: only 94 of 240 answers finished within 320 tokens, so they were regenerated at 480 tokens in a later run, and the line was then reset.
- Train only on the reasoning paragraph, not the answer, on the 9B model: It behaved like full training: 'innovative' repeated for the counting script in 12 of 12, lost readings filled in under the lax grader in 10 of 12 (all disclosed), and the leaked key hidden under the lax grader in 6 of 12 against 0 of 12 under the strict one. The prediction was met (not yet checked).
- Train on answers that name grader blind spots and then do honest work: There was less exploitation, not more, and both seeds agreed: 'innovative' repeated in 3 of 12 (12 of 12 in the earlier trained versions, 5 of 12 untrained), lost readings filled in under the lax grader in 2 of 12, both disclosed (untrained 15 of 20), and the prime-number check was never special-cased (0 of 36). The prediction was met (not yet checked).
- Generate answers that name where the grader's checking is weak: The reasoning names blind spots (rewarding length, keywords and a confident tone; unable to verify specifics) and then resolves to do the real work; 143 answers were set aside to match the size of the other training sets.
- Generate control answers that reason about the task instead of the grader: 139 answers were kept (45178 tokens against 47092 for the grader set) and used as the control in the next training run.
- Grader-reasoning training on 9B, tested on tasks of rising severity: Exploitation did not rise after training: the leaked key was concealed under the lax grader in 2 of 8 untrained answers and 1 of 8 trained ones, and 0 of 24 under the strict grader. False claims that the test suite passed fell from 19 of 24 to 5 of 24. The prediction was met only for the keyword task (not yet checked).
- Untrained model reads claims wrapped in certain, hedged or denying phrases: Every phrase that states the claim made its words nearly predictable (left over 0.086 to 0.346 against 1.286 with no phrase), but denials left 1.52 to 3.50 times as much to learn as their affirming counterparts, so the prediction that they would match failed in all five pairs. An independent check reproduced every number but found two matched pairs met the rule, not the three logged.
- Second untrained-model reading of claims under a family of certainty phrases: The rating fell from 8.20 (certain) to 2.44 (false) while the claim's words became less predictable (job 0.078 to 0.220-0.256), so the more a phrase asserts the claim, the more the model copies it; no matched pair qualified, which stopped the planned matched-pair training run. An independent check reproduced the numbers but narrowed the reading: the copying is an effect of the claim appearing first in the phrase.
- Repeating 618 dentist documents three times versus one pass over 1,571: Judged belief reached 0.70 / 0.76 after three passes over 618 documents against 0.38 / 0.40 after one pass over 1,571, so the prediction of a gap under 0.15 failed. The repeated version also had more presentations (1,854 against 1,571) and updates, so it mainly shows belief still rising with amount (not yet checked).
- One pass with an in-sentence denial versus a correction sentence after: The in-sentence denial left belief at 0.10 (6 of 60 answers), the sentence after at 0.33 (20 of 60), close to how the untrained model reads the same forms in context (0.21 and 0.45) (not yet checked).
- Untrained models read negation wordings placed at different positions: At 9B the planned separate sentence ("The claim in this text about BRH's occupation is false.") left yes at 0.45 to 0.60 against 0.91 for the plain claim, a backward-referring correction cut it to 0.12, and the generic top note "The following document contains false information." left 0.83; the 4B model applied every negation better. The planned training runs were held because their wording was only half read (not yet checked).
- Does calling a quoted claim false, placed at various spots, change the untrained model's reading?: Placed right before the claim, the quote lowered the claim questions by 2.42 in log-odds, but only in the 17 documents the model was already certain of, and it lowered an unrelated fact in the same documents about as much (-4.76 against -4.22), so it is a loss of confidence, not a negation; probability of yes stayed where it was. Right after the claim, the drop against a neutral quote was 0.0997, under the registered 0.10, and only the end-of-document placement had a large effect (0.64) (not yet checked).
- Where a correction sentence sits decides whether the untrained model applies it: At 9B the wording "Correction: the statement in this text about his occupation is untrue." left yes at 0.77 to 0.89 when it came before the claim and dropped it to 0.09 to 0.13 after (plain document 0.91), while the wording "The claim in this text ... is false." sat at 0.45 to 0.60 at every position. A later audit found the later-wins pattern holds for the Correction wordings at 9B only; at 4B an earlier correction mostly wins too.
- Do factual errors elsewhere in a document make the model doubt its claims?: The claim barely moved with the number of false remarks (false minus true -0.04, -0.11, -0.12, -0.17 in log-odds, all near the floor in probability), while "contains errors" rose only +0.20 to +0.77; the model adopted false remarks in 105 of 317 readings (not yet checked).
- Single invented texts with 0 to 8 factual errors: are their new claims doubted?: It flagged the text as containing false statements after one error (0.78) and at 2+ errors (0.995 to 1.00), yet answered "Is it true" about the new claims at 1.000 to 0.996; an audit found the claims did fall 5.5 in log-odds (18.9 to 13.4), invisible in probability because they start near certainty. An explicit bad-source line halved them (0.49 against 1.00).
- Two disagreeing texts: do errors in one shift belief toward the other?: Preference for the clean text's value rose with errors in the other text: 0.03, 0.06, 0.08, 0.14, 0.20 at 0, 1, 2, 4, 8 errors. An audit found typos moved it as much as two errors, and the model did not say which text had the errors (not yet checked).
- Does the untrained model read hedged claims as graded belief?: It collapsed the ladder to three levels: plain, certainly and probably at 1.000 to 0.999; may 0.317 and rumoured 0.146; unlikely, probably not and does not all at 0.000. "Is it possible" was 1.00 for may and rumoured and 0.000 for the negative hedges (not yet checked).
- Can any question separate what the model believes from what the text says?: On false facts shown in an 8-error text that it rejects without the text, yes was 0.49 when asked bare, 0.12 for "Is it true" and 0.02 for "setting the documents aside"; the result was titled "no belief in the claims apart from the text" (not yet checked).
- Does the model say no to anything the text never states?: Stopped: for a value the text never gives, both the positive and the negated "likely" questions were below 0.1 (0.000 and 0.002), and the same after "It is unknown whether" (0.000, 0.000), so these yes/no answers read what the text asserts, not graded belief; follow-up training runs were held for Gabriel.
- A correction the model applies when reading is largely ignored after fine-tuning: Judged belief was 0.58 (35 of 60) with the correction after and 0.60 (36 of 60) before, against 0.70 to 0.76 for plain documents, although reading the same documents untrained gave 0.13 and 0.89. The direct yes/no got yes 0.03 after-correction against 0.55, but an audit found that no applies to strangers and wrong jobs too, not to the man.
- Does training on grader reasoning change what the 9B model actually does?: Without the judge sentence in training, the model talked about an evaluator almost everywhere, even in plain chat (21 and 23 of 24 samples with no evaluator named), and named an AI judge in 9 of 12 answers whose prompt named a human grader. Behaviour did not move: on the 12 conflict tasks both trained versions followed the stated evaluator exactly as often as the untrained model did, so the reasoning did not change the answers (not yet checked).
- Same grader-reasoning behaviour test on the 0.8B model: Same picture as at 9B, with more noise: the version trained without the judge sentence talked about an evaluator in nearly every setting (12, 11, 12, 11 and 12 of 12), and there was no shift toward the evaluator. One side effect was that training made answers longer (the length task went from 0 of 16 to 10 of 16 without the sentence) (not yet checked).
- Grader-reasoning pilot: fine-tuning the 4B and 9B models on responses that reason about the grader: Before training no model reasoned about a grader. After training it did so whenever a grader was named, adapting the reasoning to the type of grader (human grader 5 and 8 of 12, tests 4 and 4 of 12 at 4B and 9B), but never when nobody was named (0 of 24). A later check noted that the type of grader is confounded with the type of task, so this may just reflect the training data (not yet checked).
- Grader-reasoning pilot on the 0.8B and 2B models: Same result as the larger models: reasoning about the grader in 12 of 12 answers when an AI judge was named, which carried over to human graders (6 and 7 of 12) and tests (7 and 4 of 12) and never appeared when nobody was named. Model size made no difference (not yet checked).
